title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for bond and end-of-lease cleaning
audience: Owners of bond and end-of-lease cleaning businesses who want more work from real estate agents and property managers that fit their service area and job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the property types you clean well (for example, two-bedroom apartments), the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and the number of exits each agency handles. An agency that handles many exits in your area is worth more than a single house across town. If you cannot state these criteria, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one. Business.gov.au suggests writing one short profile for each customer segment (24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Build a scored list of agencies and managers
instruction.body: Keep one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each agency as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. The criteria are the area, the exit volume, whether there is a decision-maker you can reach, and whether the job falls inside your insurance. Record the date and the source of each contact detail. Do not buy or scrape lists: ACMA says buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent. Do not use tenants' personal or tenancy details to make contact.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals for businesses only
instruction.body: Public tender portals list government work. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026). AusTender lists federal opportunities and sends email notices. Neither was checked for bond cleaning work, so treat them as places to look, not as proven leads. Planning permit registers, such as the City of Casey example, show development, not exits, so they are a weak signal for bond work.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message says how you found the agency, makes one verifiable observation about its published listings or service range, and offers one small next step, such as a fixed-scope written quote for a defined area. Do not overstate what you know. The ACCC found in July 2026 that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). Identify yourself and make it easy to decline.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the number of follow-ups and the gap between them before you start. Remove any agency that says no or asks you to stop, and record the request. ACMA says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. Review each month which agencies replied and turned into paid work.

procedure: Write the property types, area, price range and exit-volume criteria for the work you want.
Build the agency list, score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, and record the source of each contact detail.
Choose the public signals to check, and note the date each one was checked.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call Register and your insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit agencies first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of each month.

workedExamples.situation: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A solo cleaner covers three Melbourne suburbs. An agency there lists four two-bedroom rentals in the cleaner's area, and its general business email address is on its website.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cleaner send a sales email to the agency now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The agency fits the criteria: it is inside the service area and handles property exits. The cleaner does not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, and a shared inbox does not carry the same implied consent as a named role. The cleaner first checks whether the agency has agreed to receive messages, or has invited contact. If not, the cleaner checks the Do Not Call Register before any phone call, and the call follows the DNCR guide's hours (weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm; 2018 guide). The first contact names the public listing, says how the business learned of it, offers a fixed-scope quote for the area, and asks one question. The cleaner does not contact tenants and does not use any tenancy details.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to every agency on a broad list.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message per fit tier, and start with the strong fits.

commonErrors.error: Using tenants' personal or tenancy information to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, and never use tenancy records to contact tenants.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service you are not insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check insurance before outreach. Licence and insurance rules for bond cleaning were not researched.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix a number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence and insurance rules for bond cleaning were not researched. Check the rule for each state or territory where you work before you offer the service.

Commercial electronic messages are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent must be recorded, and that an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. The Act's text was not read for this lesson.
Check every telephone number against the Do Not Call Register before a telemarketing call. The 2018 DNCR industry guide gives the calling hours; check for updates before use.

Public listings do not by themselves permit contact. The OAIC says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules where the Privacy Act applies. Coverage for a small business depends on turnover and other factors, and was not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the properties and agencies you want before you look for them.
Use public tender portals and agency listings only as places to look. Never use tenants' details to make contact.
Gaps: agent referral channels, bond-specific lead sources and the other states' tender systems were not sourced.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which agency should you contact first?
options: One single property well outside your service area, because it looks large
An agency with many exits inside your service area that you already visit
Any agency with a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public listing shows a rental in your area. What must you not do?
options: Use the tenant's personal details to contact them
Check the listing for the agency's contact details
Confirm the agency's business consent rules before a message

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to an agency, what must you do?
options: Confirm the consent and unsubscribe requirements in current ACMA guidance
Ask the agency to like your social page first
Make the subject line as catchy as possible

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'How to identify your target market', https://business.gov.au/marketing/how-to-identify-your-target-market, 24 September 2024. Supports: write one short profile for each customer segment.

Buying for Victoria, 'How to get known', https://buyingfor.vic.gov.au/how-get-known, last updated 7 August 2026. Victoria. Supports: current and past tenders are listed; suppliers can set alerts; agencies publish annual procurement plans.

Department of Finance, 'Selling to Government' (AusTender guidance), https://sellingtogov.finance.gov.au/node/8, no date shown. Supports: suppliers can filter federal opportunities and receive email notices; awarded contracts of $10,000 or more are published.

ACMA, 'Spam: Industry obligations', https://www.acma.gov.au/theACMA/spam-industry-obligations, last updated 28 March 2019 (older source). Supports: marketing messages need consent; an unsubscribe must work for at least 30 days and be honoured within 5 business days; publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages; buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

OAIC, 'Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-7-app-7-direct-marketing, page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019 (older source). Supports: public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules.

DataVic, 'Planning Permit Application Register' (City of Casey), https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/planning-permit-application-register, metadata published 15 November 2023, last updated 5 November 2026 as shown. Victoria. Supports: some councils publish registers of planning applications with suburb and status; check your own council's register.

ACCC, 'Misleading and high pressure unsolicited sales practices widespread', https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/misleading-and-high-pressure-unsolicited-sales-practices-widespread, 28 July 2026. Supports: many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves.

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older source). Supports: telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm, not Sundays or public holidays; lists should be checked against the register.

ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04 per the research file. Supports: consent, accurate sender details, and an unsubscribe honoured within five working days.
Notes: no source in the research covers bond-specific agency channels (gap). The DNCR hours are from a 2018 guide. The tender portals were not checked for bond cleaning work.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: As recorded in the research files: consent is needed before marketing messages are sent; sender details must be accurate; each commercial message needs an unsubscribe that is honoured within five working days. Publisher: ACMA.
